questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted a big culture shock. I found that Japan was perfect combination of being safe and modern while having a very different culture that i could explore during my exchange.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. I lived in an international dorm at the university which provided info-meeting and also had local university students who could help with japanese translations.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I received assistance with registering as a temporary resident, applying for health care (which was both required) and applying for being a resident without having to pay pension. I was also provided contact information to the international office, who could help me with any issues that might arise.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: International dormitory with shared units.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: We had a floor with many cooking facilities. Sort of like an industry kitchen.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer: It's amazing for cultural exchange and meeting new people. The make a big deal out of japanese people living there as well, so its not just a hub for all the europeans. It is however on Tama campus which is in Hachioji and not very central Tokyo. It's more like a suburb, but it takes only 1 hour to Shinjuku, which is not a lot since going between the districts in the center quickly takes 40 mins.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: We were provided an excel sheets of programs in english. All we had to do was to pick the ones that interested us and post the corresponding information in an application.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The international office was surely available, but i mostly used the other students at the dorm and asked their help and reccomendations.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: There were no issues at all.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't be afraid to ask other students, they are often the ones with the knowledge you seek.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It was fairly easy. Really nothing compared to computer science at KU. I believe it is because many of the courses i took involved being able to express oneself clearly in english which is on average a lot easier for danish people than for Japanese students where the english proficiency, i found, was usually a lot lower.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was more like danish high school. You sit in a classroom (i had only one course that used a lecture hall) and you get points for attendance and participation. You even fail a class if you do not attend some specified number of times.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Data Analysis
Data Science
International Product Development
Japanese B I (2)
Japanese B II (2)
Japanese Management
Philosophy
Public Management

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Data Science was good introductory course for people who have no knowledge of computer science. The format and the teacher was great.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Make sure you have enough money to go travelling around in Japan. It's not expensive but it can be difficult to make a budget for before arriving, because a lot of travel plans happen spontaneously with other students.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food and clothing was much less expansive than i though (decent meal at a restaurant is 45 DKK). Tokyo has a rep for being an expensive place, but I think that must be the rent for living. Since i lived in a cheap dormitory everything seemed very cheap compared to danish standards.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Not very available. No one could give an overview of the university clubs, you had to know one who knew one. I tried joining clubs but the language barrier makes it very difficult and awkward for the Japanese who wants to be very welcoming. I recommend learning some Japanese before trying to join a club.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Cultural exchange programs, cooking-parties and also event-based parties were available.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go out with other exchange students and Japanese students. Do a lot of Karaoke and go to Izakayas.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Hiking is a top recommendation. Mt. Mitake and Mt. Takao are nice spots not far with train from the University.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Since the culture is so different it took some time getting used to. But everyone was nice and helpful and my Japanese roommate explained a lot of Japanese Customs for me.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Don't be shy go talk to people! The Japanese might do it first though, they are very interested in foreigners. If you are a shy person I can recommend hanging out in public areas - if you seem welcoming people will likely come talk to you.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The language is a big one. Do yourself a favor and learn some Japanese, even if you think you will never use it after your exchange. Being able to have very basic conversations with local students and people you meet on your travels makes it so much more enjoyable, to not mention the obvious practical aspect of being able to ask questions.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The helpfulness and humble attitude. It takes some time getting used to and might seem awkward at first, when you realise how crude your own behaviour might be in relation to it. But very likely you will assimilate it doing your stay and might even become more self reflective in avoidance of causing other trouble.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Stay at the International Dormitory Chuo (IRC). Having social activities and people available really enriches an exchange. It also means that you will live with Japanese, which makes immersing in the culture and getting help navigating Japan so much more easy.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I've written it before, but I will write it again. Learn some Japanese, interacting with local people is very rewarding and being able to ask for help and read signs makes everything much easier when travelling in Japan.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: My roomates. I had a Korean and Japanese roomate. They gave me a lot of insights into Korean and Japanese culture and we went and did a lot of the authentic Japanese activities, which is what you come to appreciate once you've done all the touristy-stuff. You can always come back to Japan and be a tourist, but you will (usually) never again be a student in Japan. So immerse in the Japanese Student life!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: It was clearly again the language barrier. Even though i studied Japanese and know the basics I still needed help for practical things like signing up for a gym, signing out as a resident when i had to leave etc. You might think google translate or DeepL can solve such problems but often they fall short when translating Japanese for some reason.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
